stemMd:
Consider this argument:

> Every lawyer who has argued a case before the supreme court has at least fifteen years of practice. Dr Merlo is a lawyer with twenty-two years of practice. Therefore Dr Merlo has argued a case before the supreme court.

Which of the following identifies the logical error in the argument?
instructionsMd: Both premises are to be taken as true. The question is why the conclusion does not follow from them.

options.label: A
options.textMd: It confuses the length of Dr Merlo's practice with the quality of the cases she has argued.

options.label: B
options.textMd: It treats a condition necessary for arguing before the supreme court as if it were sufficient.

options.label: C
options.textMd: It draws a conclusion about one individual lawyer from a claim about the group's average practice.

options.label: D
options.textMd: It generalises from a sample of lawyers too small to support its rule about fifteen years of practice.

explanationMd:
Write the first premise as an arrow and watch which way it points:

$$\text{argued before the supreme court} \Rightarrow \text{at least fifteen years of practice}$$

Fifteen years is therefore a **necessary** condition for having argued there — a gate everyone must pass. The argument then finds that Dr Merlo has passed the gate and concludes she is inside. That runs the arrow backwards: it treats the necessary condition as though it were **sufficient** — exactly the error described by the choice about treating a necessary condition as if it were sufficient.

The premise is perfectly compatible with a profession in which thousands of lawyers have twenty-two years of practice and only a handful have ever appeared before the supreme court. Nothing in it says that long practice produces such an appearance.

**How to check.** Build a counter-model — a world where both premises are true and the conclusion is false. Take a bar in which every supreme-court advocate has twenty-five years of practice, and Dr Merlo, with her twenty-two years, has spent her career in tax tribunals. Premise 1 holds, premise 2 holds, the conclusion fails. A valid argument admits no such world, so the argument is invalid, and the option naming the direction of the error is the answer.

distractorRationale.c: No average appears anywhere. The first premise is a universal claim — *every* such lawyer has at least fifteen years — not a claim about the group's typical or mean length of practice, so the familiar average-to-individual fallacy is not what is going wrong here.
distractorRationale.a: The argument says nothing about the quality of the cases Dr Merlo has argued; both premises and the conclusion are about years of practice and about whether an appearance occurred. Reading a quality claim into it imports a concern the argument never raises.
distractorRationale.d: The rule about fifteen years of practice is asserted as a universal premise, not inferred from any sample. There is no inductive step to criticise; the fault lies entirely in how the rule is applied to Dr Merlo, not in how the rule was arrived at.

accessibilityText: A logical-error question. The argument runs: every lawyer who has argued before the supreme court has at least fifteen years of practice; Dr Merlo is a lawyer with twenty-two years of practice; therefore Dr Merlo has argued before the supreme court. Four candidate descriptions of the error follow. The explanation restates the first premise as an arrow from 'argued before the supreme court' to 'at least fifteen years of practice'.

provenance.notes: Original item written to the published syllabus entry 'identifying logical errors in an argument'. Dr Merlo and the argument are invented.

review.author: bocconi-law-topup-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The premise gives fifteen years of practice as necessary for having argued before the supreme court; the argument infers the converse from Merlo meeting the condition, treating necessary as sufficient. Quality of cases is not mentioned, the premise is universal not an average, and no sample is involved, so the other options misdescribe the argument. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-cue-batch1-run1) reached the same answer: The premise says arguing before the supreme court implies at least fifteen years of practice; the argument reverses it, treating fifteen-plus years as enough to conclude she argued there, i.e. treating a necessary condition as sufficient. Quality of cases, a group average and sample size are not features of the argument.]

review.notes: Author confirmed a counter-model in which both premises hold and the conclusion fails, and checked that the choices about a group average, about the quality of Dr Merlo's cases and about a small sample each name a fault the argument does not commit (no average, no quality claim, no inductive step).
